chunks.title: FORMULA 1 BASICS AND ESSENTIAL GUIDE
chunks.content: # FORMULA 1 BASICS AND ESSENTIAL GUIDE

chunks.title: What is Formula 1?
chunks.content:
## What is Formula 1?
Formula 1 (F1) is the highest class of international open-wheel, single-seater auto racing sanctioned by the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA). It is considered the pinnacle of motorsport and automotive engineering.

chunks.title: Key Terminology & Concepts
chunks.content:
## Key Terminology & Concepts
- Apex: The innermost point of the racing line through a corner. Hitting the apex allows the driver to carry maximum speed and achieve the optimal exit trajectory.
- Understeer: When a car does not turn as much as the steering angle demands, causing the front tyres to slide outwards. Often described as "the front of the car pushes wide".
- Oversteer: When the rear tyres lose traction before the front, causing the rear end to swing outwards. Often described as "the back end stepping out".
- Downforce: Aerodynamic downward thrust created by the front wing, floor (ground effect tunnels), and rear wing. Downforce presses tyres into the asphalt to increase grip in high-speed corners.
- Slipstream / Tow: Following closely behind a leading car where air resistance is lower, allowing higher top speed on straightaways before overtaking.
- Dirty Air: Disturbed, turbulent air trailing behind an F1 car that reduces aerodynamic downforce and cooling efficiency for cars following closely.
- Box: The team radio call instructing the driver to enter the pit lane for a tyre change or pit stop ("Box, box, box").
- Pit Stop: A lightning-fast team stop where 20+ crew members change all four tyres in as little as 1.8 to 2.5 seconds, adjust wing angles, and repair front wing assemblies if needed.
- Telemetry: Real-time wireless data transmitted from hundreds of car sensors (throttle, brake pressure, tyre temps, engine RPM, G-forces, suspension travel) directly to team pit wall and engineers.

chunks.title: Teams and Constructors
chunks.content:
## Teams and Constructors
- F1 consists of 10 constructor teams, each entering 2 cars (20 drivers in total).
- Teams build their own custom chassis and aerodynamic packages, and either build or purchase power units (Ferrari, Mercedes, Red Bull Powertrains-Honda, Renault/Alpine).

chunks.title: Circuits
chunks.content:
## Circuits
- F1 races take place on purpose-built permanent race tracks (e.g., Silverstone, Spa-Francorchamps, Monza) and temporary street circuits (e.g., Monaco, Singapore, Las Vegas, Baku, Jeddah).

chunks.title: DRAG REDUCTION SYSTEM (DRS) IN FORMULA 1
chunks.content: # DRAG REDUCTION SYSTEM (DRS) IN FORMULA 1

chunks.title: What is DRS?
chunks.content:
## What is DRS?
DRS stands for Drag Reduction System. It is a driver-controlled aerodynamic device introduced by the FIA in 2011 to promote overtaking and enhance racing excitement in Formula 1.

chunks.title: How Does DRS Work Mechanically?
chunks.content:
## How Does DRS Work Mechanically?
- The rear wing of a modern F1 car has an adjustable upper flap.
- When activated by the driver (via a steering wheel button), a hydraulic actuator lifts the flap, opening a maximum 85 mm slot between the main plane and the upper flap.
- This significantly reduces aerodynamic drag (air resistance) at the rear of the car, allowing the car to gain an estimated 10 to 12 km/h (6 to 7.5 mph) in straight-line top speed.
- When the driver touches the brake pedal, the flap immediately snaps shut to restore full aerodynamic downforce for braking stability.

chunks.title: Rules and Conditions for DRS Activation in a Race
chunks.content:
## Rules and Conditions for DRS Activation in a Race
1. Detection Point: The track has designated DRS Detection Points before long straight sections. If a chasing car is within 1.000 second behind the car ahead at the detection point, DRS is enabled for the upcoming activation zone.
2. Activation Zone: The driver can open the rear wing flap only within the designated DRS Activation Zone marked on the track.
3. Lap Eligibility: DRS is activated after Lap 1 (or 1 lap after a Safety Car / Virtual Safety Car restart, updated from the traditional 2 laps).
4. Weather Conditions: Race Control disables DRS if weather conditions turn wet or visibility is poor.
5. Yellow Flags: DRS is automatically disabled in any sector under yellow flag conditions.
6. Lapped Cars: DRS can also be activated when following a lapped car within 1.0 second.
7. Defending Car: A defending car cannot use DRS unless it is also within 1.0 second of another car ahead (creating a "DRS train").

chunks.title: DRS in Practice and Qualifying Sessions
chunks.content:
## DRS in Practice and Qualifying Sessions
- In Free Practice and Qualifying sessions, drivers can activate DRS in all designated DRS zones at any time, regardless of the gap to other cars.

chunks.title: ENERGY RECOVERY SYSTEM (ERS) IN FORMULA 1
chunks.content: # ENERGY RECOVERY SYSTEM (ERS) IN FORMULA 1

chunks.title: What is ERS?
chunks.content:
## What is ERS?
ERS stands for Energy Recovery System. It is an integral component of modern Formula 1 hybrid turbo power units (introduced in 2014) that harvests waste kinetic and thermal energy and converts it into electrical power to boost engine performance.

chunks.title: Key Components of the F1 Power Unit & ERS
chunks.content:
## Key Components of the F1 Power Unit & ERS
1. Internal Combustion Engine (ICE): 1.6-litre turbocharged 90-degree V6 engine delivering around 750 to 800 bhp at up to 15,000 RPM.
2. MGU-K (Motor Generator Unit - Kinetic):
   - Connected directly to the crankshaft of the engine.
   - During braking, it acts as a generator, recovering kinetic energy that would otherwise be lost as heat.
   - Under acceleration, it acts as a motor, deploying up to 120 kW (approx. 160 horsepower) directly to the drivetrain.
   - Maximum 2 MJ of energy per lap can be recovered into the Energy Store via the MGU-K, and up to 4 MJ per lap can be deployed from the Energy Store to the MGU-K.
3. MGU-H (Motor Generator Unit - Heat):
   - Connected to the turbocharger between the exhaust turbine and compressor.
   - Converts heat energy from exhaust gases into electrical power.
   - Can either send energy directly to the Energy Store (battery) or directly to the MGU-K to eliminate turbo lag.
   - Energy recovery and transfer from the MGU-H is unlimited by the regulations.
4. Energy Store (ES):
   - High-performance lithium-ion battery pack weighing between 20 kg and 25 kg.
   - Stores harvested electrical energy for deployment.
5. Control Electronics (CE):
   - Manages the complex power flow between the ICE, MGU-K, MGU-H, and Energy Store millions of times per second.

chunks.title: ERS Deployment Modes
chunks.content:
## ERS Deployment Modes
- Hotlap / Qualifying Mode: Maximum electrical power deployment over a single flying lap.
- Race Mode / Balanced Mode: Strategic energy harvesting and deployment to maintain battery state of charge (SoC) over a full race stint.
- Overtake Button / Push-to-Pass: A steering wheel button that allows the driver to dump maximum available electrical energy (160 bhp) on straightaways for defending or attacking.
- Recharge / Harvest Mode (Clipping / Lift-and-Coast): Slowing down energy output at the end of long straights to replenish battery reserves.

chunks.title: FORMULA 1 OFFICIAL RULES AND REGULATIONS
chunks.content: # FORMULA 1 OFFICIAL RULES AND REGULATIONS

chunks.title: 1. Race Weekend Format
chunks.content:
## 1. Race Weekend Format
- A standard Formula 1 race weekend takes place across three days: Friday, Saturday, and Sunday.
- Friday: Free Practice 1 (FP1) and Free Practice 2 (FP2), each lasting 60 minutes.
- Saturday: Free Practice 3 (FP3) lasting 60 minutes, followed by Qualifying.
- Sunday: The Grand Prix race (approx. 305 km or 2 hours maximum time limit, with Monaco being 260 km).

chunks.title: 2. Qualifying Format (Knockout System)
chunks.content:
## 2. Qualifying Format (Knockout System)
- Q1 (18 minutes): All 20 cars participate. The 5 slowest cars are eliminated and take grid positions 16 to 20.
- Q2 (15 minutes): The remaining 15 cars participate. The 5 slowest cars are eliminated and take grid positions 11 to 15.
- Q3 (12 minutes): The top 10 cars compete for Pole Position (1st on the grid) down to 10th.

chunks.title: 3. Sprint Weekend Format
chunks.content:
## 3. Sprint Weekend Format
- Friday: Free Practice 1 (60 mins) followed by Sprint Qualifying (SQ1, SQ2, SQ3).
- Saturday: Sprint Race (100 km, approx. 30 mins) followed by main Grand Prix Qualifying.
- Sunday: The Grand Prix race.

chunks.title: 4. Track Flags and Meanings
chunks.content:
## 4. Track Flags and Meanings
- Green Flag: Track is clear, racing conditions resumed.
- Yellow Flag (Single): Danger ahead, reduce speed, no overtaking allowed.
- Double Yellow Flag: Great danger ahead, reduce speed significantly, prepare to change direction or stop.
- Red Flag: Session suspended immediately. All cars must reduce speed and return to the pit lane.
- Blue Flag: Warns a slower or lapped car that a faster car is approaching and must be allowed to pass.
- Black and White Flag (diagonal): Unsportsmanlike conduct warning for track limits or dangerous driving.
- Black Flag with Car Number: Driver is disqualified and must return to the pits immediately.
- Chequered Flag: Session or race is finished.

chunks.title: 5. Safety Car (SC) and Virtual Safety Car (VSC)
chunks.content:
## 5. Safety Car (SC) and Virtual Safety Car (VSC)
- Safety Car (SC): Deployed by race control for serious incidents. A physical Aston Martin or Mercedes-AMG safety car leads the pack. Overtaking is prohibited. Lapped cars may be instructed to unlap themselves before restart.
- Virtual Safety Car (VSC): Imposed when track marshals or minor hazards require speed reduction without physical safety car. Drivers must reduce speed and maintain minimum sector delta times.

chunks.title: 6. Penalties and Infringements
chunks.content:
## 6. Penalties and Infringements
- 5-Second Time Penalty: Added to pit stop time or final race time (for track limits, minor collisions).
- 10-Second Time Penalty: Added to pit stop time or final race time for more severe infractions.
- Drive-Through Penalty: Driver must drive through the pit lane at limited speed without stopping.
- 10-Second Stop-and-Go Penalty: Driver must enter the pit lane, stop in their pit box for 10 seconds without mechanics touching the car, and then rejoin.
- Grid Drop Penalty: Dropping places on the starting grid for engine/gearbox component replacements exceeding season allocation.

chunks.title: 7. Parc Fermé
chunks.content:
## 7. Parc Fermé
- Parc Fermé regulations come into effect once cars leave the pit lane during qualifying. Teams are strictly forbidden from modifying car setups, suspension, or aerodynamics, allowing only routine maintenance, tyre changes, and minor front wing angle adjustments.

chunks.title: FORMULA 1 POINTS SYSTEM AND CHAMPIONSHIPS
chunks.content: # FORMULA 1 POINTS SYSTEM AND CHAMPIONSHIPS

chunks.title: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview
Formula 1 awards championship points to drivers and constructors based on their finishing positions in Grand Prix races and Sprint races throughout the season.

chunks.title: Grand Prix Race Points (Full Race Distance)
chunks.content:
## Grand Prix Race Points (Full Race Distance)
Points are awarded to the top 10 finishers in every full Grand Prix:
- 1st Place (Winner): 25 points
- 2nd Place: 18 points
- 3rd Place: 15 points
- 4th Place: 12 points
- 5th Place: 10 points
- 6th Place: 8 points
- 7th Place: 6 points
- 8th Place: 4 points
- 9th Place: 2 points
- 10th Place: 1 point
- Positions 11 to 20: 0 points

chunks.title: Fastest Lap Bonus Point
chunks.content:
## Fastest Lap Bonus Point
- 1 bonus point is awarded to the driver who sets the fastest official lap of the Grand Prix, PROVIDED that driver finishes in the top 10 (positions 1st through 10th).
- If the driver with fastest lap finishes in 11th or lower (or DNFs), no fastest lap point is awarded to anyone for that race.

chunks.title: Sprint Race Points
chunks.content:
## Sprint Race Points
Points are awarded to the top 8 finishers in the 100 km Sprint race:
- 1st Place: 8 points
- 2nd Place: 7 points
- 3rd Place: 6 points
- 4th Place: 5 points
- 5th Place: 4 points
- 6th Place: 3 points
- 7th Place: 2 points
- 8th Place: 1 point

chunks.title: Shortened Races (Sliding Scale after Spa 2021)
chunks.content:
## Shortened Races (Sliding Scale after Spa 2021)
If a race is stopped and cannot be resumed:
1. Less than 25% distance completed: Points awarded to top 5 (6, 4, 3, 2, 1).
2. 25% to 50% distance completed: Points awarded to top 9 (13, 10, 8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1).
3. 50% to 75% distance completed: Points awarded to top 10 (19, 14, 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1).
4. Over 75% distance completed: Full 100% points awarded.

chunks.title: Championships
chunks.content:
## Championships
- World Drivers' Championship (WDC): Total individual points accumulated across the entire season by a driver. The highest total wins the world championship.
- World Constructors' Championship (WCC): Sum of points scored by both cars / drivers of each constructor (team) across the season. Prize money allocation is distributed according to final WCC standings.

chunks.title: PIRELLI FORMULA 1 TYRES AND REGULATIONS
chunks.content: # PIRELLI FORMULA 1 TYRES AND REGULATIONS

chunks.title: Tyre Supplier
chunks.content:
## Tyre Supplier
Pirelli is the sole official tyre supplier for Formula 1. F1 uses 18-inch low-profile wheels and tyres.

chunks.title: Slick (Dry-Weather) Compounds
chunks.content:
## Slick (Dry-Weather) Compounds
Pirelli manufactures five to six slick compounds numbered from C0 to C5 (with C1 being the hardest and C5/C6 being the softest):
- Hard Compound (White Sidewall): Slowest warm-up time, lowest peak grip, but longest lifespan and highest resistance to degradation. Ideal for abrasive tracks and hot ambient temperatures.
- Medium Compound (Yellow Sidewall): The balanced, versatile compound offering a compromise between speed and endurance.
- Soft Compound (Red Sidewall): Maximum grip and fastest lap time, rapid warm-up, but prone to thermal degradation and graining over longer stints. Used primarily for qualifying and aggressive race strategies.

chunks.title: Slick (Dry-Weather) Compounds
chunks.content: For each race weekend, Pirelli selects three distinct compounds from their range and labels them White (Hard), Yellow (Medium), and Red (Soft).

chunks.title: Wet-Weather Compounds
chunks.content:
## Wet-Weather Compounds
- Intermediate (Green Sidewall): Designed for damp, standing-water-free, or drying tracks. Grooved tread displaces approx. 30 litres of water per second per tyre at 300 km/h.
- Full Wet (Blue Sidewall): Deeply grooved tread for heavy rainfall and severe standing water. Displaces approx. 85 litres of water per second per tyre at 300 km/h to prevent aquaplaning.

chunks.title: Mandatory Race Tyre Rules
chunks.content:
## Mandatory Race Tyre Rules
1. Mandatory Two-Compound Rule: In a dry race, each driver MUST use at least two different dry slick compounds (e.g., Medium to Hard, Soft to Hard). This makes at least one pit stop mandatory.
2. Wet Race Exemption: If Intermediate or Full Wet tyres are used at any point during a race, the mandatory two-compound rule is waived, and drivers are not forced to make a pit stop (though usually they do).
3. Weekend Tyre Allocation: Each driver receives 13 sets of dry tyres (usually 8 Soft, 3 Medium, 2 Hard), 4 sets of Intermediates, and 3 sets of Wets per race weekend.

chunks.title: Tyre Degradation and Performance Factors
chunks.content:
## Tyre Degradation and Performance Factors
- Thermal Degradation: Overheating tyre surface and carcass causing loss of grip.
- Graining: Small rubber bits tearing from the tread and sticking to the surface, reducing surface contact.
- Blistering: Excessive core heat causing rubber below the surface to vaporize and break away.
- Tyre Blankets: Pre-heating tyres in the pit garage (currently limited to 70°C for slicks) to ensure immediate operating temperature upon exiting the pits.
